items.title: California targets Nvidia in China AI chip probe
items.summary: The probe by California, where the AI chipmaker has its global headquarters, follows former CEO Jensen Huang's departure.
items.content:
By Lily Jamali North America Technology correspondent
California has served an investigative subpoena on the AI chip designer Nvidia in the wake of a scandal that ended in the departure of longtime CEO Jensen Huang.
The state's top law enforcement officer, attorney general Rob Bonta, said he is probing whether Nvidia or Huang's actions resulted in China obtaining advanced chips or confidential information, adding that such actions could violate California law if the company is found to have mislead investors and the public.
"Nvidia is in a messy, transnational situation but the underlying principle of our corporate securities law is clear: Companies cannot mislead their investors," Bonta said on Thursday.
Figure caption, How could the Nvidia CEOâs affair threaten US national security?
Nvidia has its global headquarters in Santa Clara, California.
Earlier this month, it emerged that Huang had an extramarital relationship with a suspected Chinese spy, Alice Huang, who was an executive at the Singapore-based data centre company Megaspeed.
Some members of the US Congress have urged the Department of Commerce to investigate whether Megaspeed, a major Nvidia customer, diverted Nvidia chips to China.
Megaspeed has previously said it is aware of reports "containing assertions about our business, supply chain and global operations that are not supported by verifiable evidence".
Nvidia shares have plummeted 22% since the New York Times reported on the affair in early November.
Earlier this week, the company's board chair Harvey Jones said Nvidia had no intention of reinstating Jensen Huang after the longtime Nvidia boss and co-founder issued a statement saying he would be "honoured" to return, as some tech leaders including Elon Musk campaigned on his behalf.
Huang has acknowledged engaging in extramarital affairs â and left the company last week after reports that he had relationships with subordinates.

IEA sees potential for looser oil, LNG markets after Hormuz crisis
The IEA says oil and gas markets could face abundant supply and lower prices if Middle East disruptions ease, but recovery timing and scale remain uncertain.
Global oil and natural gas markets could face a period of more abundant supply and lower prices once disruptions in the Middle East ease, although the timing and extent of any recovery remain uncertain, according to the International Energy Agency's (IEA) World Energy Outlook 2026.
The outlook points to sharply different demand trajectories depending on how governments respond to the 2026 energy crisis. Under IEA's Stated Policies Scenario (STEPS), global oil demand levels off at around 103 million b/d by 2030 before declining gradually, while natural gas demand continues growing until the mid-2030s. Under the Current Policies Scenario (CPS), consumption of both fuels continues to increase.
The projections assume that constraints on Gulf oil and gas exports will ease into 2027 and that conditions will allow unimpeded transit through the Strait of Hormuz by end-2027. IEA cautioned that the scenarios are not forecasts and that considerable uncertainty remains over the duration of the crisis and the future of Middle East exports.
The disruption to energy flows through the Strait of Hormuz has resulted in cumulative losses of 2.8 billion bbl of oil and 60 billion cu m (bcm) of natural gas supply from the Gulf. At its peak, global oil supply fell by 16.1 million b/d from pre-conflict levels.
Ample inventories, increased production and exports from non-Gulf suppliers, alternative export routes, and reduced Chinese crude imports helped cushion the initial impact. IEA member countries also coordinated the release of 400 million bbl of emergency oil stocks, announced Mar. 11, 2026.
As inventories declined and supply disruptions continued, however, higher prices increasingly weighed on consumption. Diesel markets have been particularly strained, with prices exceeding $200/bbl amid disruptions to Middle Eastern product exports and reduced Russian supplies.
IEA's November 2026 Oil Market Report expects global oil demand to decline by around 2.7 million b/d in 2026, its first annual decrease since 2020. Natural gas demand is expected to fall by around 1.5%, or 65 bcm.
IEA's longer-term projections differ considerably across scenarios.
In the CPS, which considers policies and regulations already in place, global oil demand rises to around 106 million b/d in 2035 and 114 million b/d by 2050. Reduced passenger car consumption from electrification, efficiency improvements, and biofuels is more than offset by rising demand from petrochemicals, aviation, and heavy freight trucks.
In the STEPS, which also accounts for formally proposed policies and government strategies, oil demand levels off at around 103 million b/d by 2030 before declining to 102 million b/d in 2035 and 96 million b/d by 2050.
The Additional Response Case (ARC) examines further measures under consideration by governments to reduce import dependence, diversify energy supplies, and accelerate electrification. Oil demand in this case is more than 4 million b/d below the STEPS level by 2035 and falls to 85 million b/d by 2050.
The differences in demand are reflected in IEA's oil price projections. Under the CPS, crude prices reach $85/bbl in 2035 and $106/bbl in 2050, compared with $75/bbl and $70/bbl, respectively, in the STEPS. The ARC puts prices at $72/bbl in 2035 and $62/bbl in 2050.
Natural gas markets face a similar divergence, with a major expansion in LNG export capacity expected over the next decade.
Around 350 bcm of new LNG supply is set to enter global markets between 2025 and 2035. The US leads the expansion, and IEA estimates that LNG supply capacity could increase by more than 50% if all planned projects proceed.
In the CPS, stronger gas consumption absorbs the new LNG supply, requiring prices in major importing markets to rise again in the 2030s to support additional investment.
Under the STEPS, slower demand growth leaves an LNG supply overhang that persists for longer. Gas demand levels off at around 4,800 bcm from the 2030s onward, and excess supply pushes import prices toward the short-run marginal cost of supply.
The imbalance could be more pronounced in the ARC. Persistent uncertainty over Middle East exports leads price-sensitive Asian importers to rely more heavily on domestic energy resources and invest less in LNG import terminals, pipelines, and other gas infrastructure. If Middle East supplies subsequently recover and exporters proceed with their expansion plans, IEA sees the potential for a large and lasting LNG surplus.
By 2050, global natural gas demand reaches approximately 5,800 bcm in the CPS, compared with around 4,800 bcm in the STEPS and 4,100 bcm in the ARC.
Despite the possibility of weaker prices, IEA expects continued upstream investment to be necessary to replace declining production from existing fields.
Oil and gas fields naturally decline at around 8-9% annually, with generally higher rates outside the Middle East. Nearly 90% of the $550 billion invested annually in upstream oil and gas over the past 5 years has gone toward offsetting production declines rather than meeting demand growth.
Global upstream investment is estimated at around $550 billion in 2026, about 1% above 2025, while the IEA Upstream Capital Cost Index is expected to increase by around 8%.
Additional production could come from countries including the United Arab Emirates (UAE) and Venezuela. The UAE, which left OPEC in May 2026, plans to expand crude production capacity to 5 million b/d by 2027. Its production reaches 5.8 million b/d in 2035 under the STEPS.
Venezuelan production is projected to rise to 1.5 million b/d by 2035 in the STEPS, supported by around $70 billion in cumulative investment to refurbish existing facilities and develop new fields.
IEA estimates that even in the ARC, where oil and gas demand declines, around 9 million b/d of new oil projects and 500 bcm of new natural gas projects will be required by 2035 to offset declining output from existing fields.

items.title: Israeli military completes ground operation in Gaza beyond Yellow Line
items.summary: Hamas condemned the incursion, which the Israeli military said was to dismantle a "terror tunnel", as a "flagrant" ceasefire violation.
items.content:
Image caption, Residents fled the area near Nuseirat and Bureij refugee camps following the Israeli evacuation order
By David Gritten ,Â  Benedict Garman Â  and Â  Emma Pengelly ,Â  BBC Verify
Israeli forces have completed a rare ground operation in part of central Gaza outside their control, the military says, a day after residents were ordered to evacuate.
Families fled their homes and tents on Wednesday as tanks advanced into an area east of Nuseirat refugee camp and onto the territory's main north-south road under the cover of artillery strikes.
The Israeli military said the "targeted" operation aimed to dismantle a "terror tunnel" west of the so-called Yellow Line, which marks the more than 60% of Gaza's territory occupied by Israel.
The Palestinian armed group Hamas, which controls the rest of Gaza, accused Israel of a "flagrant violation" of the October 2025 ceasefire deal.
Violence has continued in Gaza over the past 13 months, with near-daily Israeli strikes, and living conditions for the 2.1 million people there remain dire.
Wednesday's Israeli incursion deep beyond the Yellow Line was reportedly the first to be publicly announced by the Israel Defense Forces (IDF) since the ceasefire began.
In the early afternoon, Israeli military body Cogat's Arabic spokesperson announced the start of the operation and warned Palestinians living in an area north of Nuseirat and Bureij refugee camp to stay away for their own safety. It also said a section of Salah al-Din road that passed through the area would be closed to traffic.
In the evening, the IDF said the joint operation with the Shin Bet security service sought "to dismantle a terror tunnel west of the Yellow Line that posed an immediate and direct threat to IDF troops".
On Thursday morning, Cogat told Palestinians on social media that "the activity has ended, and the Salah al-Din axis has been reopened".
Hamas warned in a statement that the advance of Israeli military vehicles beyond the Yellow Line and the evacuation of residents constituted "a dangerous development and a flagrant violation of the ceasefire agreement".
Gaza's Hamas-run government media office meanwhile said that an estimated 6,000 people had fled their homes and tents because of the operation, and that this amounted to the war crime of forced displacement.
Footage published by Palestinian media outlets and on social media showed dozens of families fleeing areas near Nuseirat camp following the Israeli evacuation order.
In one video verified by BBC Verify, a man could be seen ducking after hearing artillery fire and then running along Salah al-Din road, about 1.5km (0.9 miles) west of the Yellow Line. "The Israeli occupation now is firing randomly near the houses and tents of people," he said.
An image, meanwhile, showed six armoured vehicles, including tanks and bulldozers, around Salah al-Din road.
A resident of Nuseirat who was forced to flee told BBC Arabic's Middle East Daily programme: "The situation is now extremely dire, with Israeli forces firing indiscriminately at areas where displaced people have sought shelter."
"We couldn't take any of our belongings with us - not even our blankets, pillows, or clothes. We had no choice but to leave everything behind."
A second resident also reported "indiscriminate gunfire and shelling" and said there had been "numerous casualties, including fatalities".
Asked about those reports, the IDF sent a general statement about the operation.
Multiple verified videos of the aftermath of the incursion on Thursday showed destruction, earth banks, and heavy vehicle tracks more than 1.2km beyond the Yellow Line.
That is believed to be the furthest Israeli troops have advanced into central Gaza since they occupied the so-called Netzarim Corridor before the ceasefire.
Some residents returned to check their properties following the Israeli withdrawal.
"The entire area has been destroyed, and we honestly do not know what to do," Abd Aliwa told Reuters news agency as he sat beside a pile of rubble.

Israel moves Yellow Line deeper into Gaza, satellite images show
Gaza's Hamas-run Civil Defence agency said three people were killed and others were wounded in three separate Israeli drone strikes on Wednesday.
One man was killed in Nuseirat, the second was killed to the north in Gaza City, and the third was killed in the central town of Deir al-Balah, it added.
The IDF told the BBC that it had "struck several military operatives".
Gaza health officials said another two people were killed on Thursday by Israeli fire in eastern Gaza City, according to Reuters. There was no immediate comment from the IDF.
At least 1,662 people have been killed in Israeli attacks in Gaza since the ceasefire began last year, according to the territory's Hamas-run health ministry, whose figures are considered reliable by the UN.
The Israeli military says six of its soldiers have been killed over the same period.
Meanwhile, more than 1.9 million people - about 90% of Gaza's population - remain displaced, with 1.4 million of them living in tents or makeshift shelters, according to the UN.
Reconstruction has yet to begin in Gaza, where an estimated 82% of all structures have been destroyed or damaged during the war, as US President Donald Trump's peace plan has largely stalled.
The disarmament of Hamas has been a key sticking point.
The group has agreed to give up its weapons in exchange for a phased withdrawal of Israeli troops from the 60% of Gaza they currently occupy. But Israel has insisted that Hamas must fully disarm before any pullout.
The war was triggered by the Hamas-led attack on southern Israel on 7 October 2023, when about 1,200 people were killed and 251 others were taken hostage.
Since then, more than 74,710 people have been killed in Israeli attacks in Gaza, its health ministry says.

items.title: Ukraine war briefing: Trump ‘open’ to Kyiv getting Nato-like mutual defence guarantee, says Kushner - The Guardian
items.summary: Ukraine war briefing: Trump ‘open’ to Kyiv getting Nato-like mutual defence guarantee, says Kushner  <font color="#6f6f6f"
items.content:
A police officer speaks with the owners of a damaged apartment at the site of a residential building hit by a Russian drone strike in Kyiv, Ukraine, on Thursday. Photograph: Valentyn Ogirenko/Reuters
A police officer speaks with the owners of a damaged apartment at the site of a residential building hit by a Russian drone strike in Kyiv, Ukraine, on Thursday. Photograph: Valentyn Ogirenko/Reuters
Ukraine war briefing: Trump ‘open’ to Kyiv getting Nato-like mutual defence guarantee, says Kushner
US envoy also says he believes Moscow is ‘comfortable’ with a guarantee; Russia attacks Kyiv bridges after Putin vows response for Crimea bridge attack. What we know on day 1,731
US envoy Jared Kushner has said Donald Trump is open to extending Ukraine a security guarantee similar to Nato’s mutual defence clause , but stressed that Washington has to protect its interests too. French president Emmanuel Macron meanwhile urged Kyiv’s allies to “reopen the question” of Ukraine becoming a member of the military alliance. Kushner, Trump’s son-in-law, told a press conference in Germany: “From America’s perspective, giving an Article 5-like security guarantee is a really, really big deal. And I think that that’s something that President Trump is open to, but obviously it has to be in America’s interest to do that. We also have to make sure that it’s part of a broader security package.”
Kushner’s comments came after Ukraine’s allies gathered for a summit of the “coalition of the willing” in Berlin with Volodymyr Zelenskyy to emphasise support for Kyiv nearly five years since Russia’s 2022 invasion, and to push for a European role in future peace negotiations. Kushner added on Thursday that “we’ve gotten the Russians comfortable with that concept, where any security guarantee for Ukraine would be based on Article 5 ”. He noted that went with Moscow’s intention to “not have another war” when this conflict was over, while acknowledging “scepticism” over the position.
Macron called on Ukraine’s allies to do the “maximum” to deliver the air defence systems it needed, as well as looking again at Ukraine joining Nato . “Faced with the maximalist nature of the Russian position, I believe we need to reopen the question of Ukraine’s accession to Nato,” the French president said in Berlin. “Everyone who has the capacity to provide the means to defend and protect Ukrainian citizens must do so now,” he said, adding the priority was to deploy anti-missile systems and interceptors.
Vladimir Putin said Russia’s response to the bombing of the Kerch bridge to Crimea would be “painful” , after Ukraine attacked the strategic connection for the third time this week. The Russian president claimed he had considered agreeing to local ceasefires until the Kerch road bridge was destroyed, report Dan Sabbagh and Jakub Krupa .
On Friday, after Putin’s threat, a Russian ballistic missile attack hit three ⁠bridges on Kyiv’s Dnipro River and killed three people , the city’s mayor said, in the ⁠biggest strikes on routes ⁠connecting ​the left and right banks of Ukraine’s capital since the war began. The missiles hit the ⁠ Podilsko-Voskresenskyi bridge crossing as well as the Darnytskyi and Pivdennyi bridges , Vitali Klitschko said on Telegram, resulting in closure or ⁠traffic restrictions. About ‌15 people were injured, he added. The strikes also caused fires ‌and damaged critical infrastructure and buildings. In the north-eastern city of Kharkiv, a Russian drone damaged a hospital, wounding four people, mayor Igor Terekhov said. In ‌Russian-controlled Luhansk, three ⁠people ​were ⁠killed ⁠in ​a Ukrainian ‌attack, said Russian-installed ‌authorities of ​the ⁠eastern Ukrainian ​region.
The summit of the coalition of the willing on Thursday was co-hosted by the leaders of Germany, Britain and France shortly after unprecedented three-way talks in China between Trump, Putin and Chinese leader Xi Jinping. China, Russia and the US said after their talks they had agreed to a peace statement, but the declaration made no mention of the war in Ukraine. The European coalition’s meeting in Berlin expressed indignation at the trilateral’s cosy optics, reports Rebecca Bailey . “Mr Putin is not our friend and ⁠will never be,” the Polish prime minister, Donald Tusk, said in a rejoinder to Trump.
German chancellor Friedrich Merz said he expected new Ukraine peace talks would “take place soon” , with Europe now set to have a seat at the table alongside the US, Russia and Ukraine. Merz, speaking in Berlin, did not give a date and added that “we are looking for locations on neutral ground”, naming the United Arab Emirates as a possible location. British prime minister Andy Burnham said: “I hope that message is heard very clearly in Moscow. For as long as it takes, we will be there at the side of Ukraine and we will not falter.”
A wave of daytime Russian strikes on Kyiv on Thursday killed one person and damaged the historic Saint Volodymyr Cathedral as well as the embassies of Austria and the Netherlands. “Russia has been terrorising Kyiv with drones all day ... At least four people are known to be injured so far, and one person was killed,” prime minister Sergiy Koretsky said.

Hormuz Oil Exports Could Decline amid Inbound Tanker Shortage
The increased flows of oil from the Strait of Hormuz, mostly thanks to ship-to-ship (STS) transfers in the Gulf of Oman, are tying up supertankers for weeks waiting for the transfers outside the Strait
The market and most analysts assume that the steady flow of crude oil from the Strait of Hormuz and the entire Middle Eastern region will continue into the next months.
Analysts are touting the remarkable recovery in crude oil exports from the Persian Gulf, which have jumped close to pre-war levels in recent months.
The oil market reflects the bearish sentiment, with Brent Crude prices sliding in the past weeks to around $92 per barrel, down from a recent peak of over $118 per barrel in late October.
The market and most analysts assume that the steady flow of crude oil from the Strait of Hormuz and the entire Middle Eastern region will continue into the next months, rebalancing supply and demand and even tipping the balance into a large surplus next year.
However, in the volatile situation in and around the Strait of Hormuz, with no recent rapprochement for potential U.S.-Iran talks, nothing is given, and no forecast has more than 50/50 odds of panning out.
The Iran war has reshuffled trade routes and patterns and tied up more tankers in inefficient and lengthy voyages.
The increased flows of oil from the Strait of Hormuz, mostly thanks to ship-to-ship (STS) transfers in the Gulf of Oman, are tying up supertankers for weeks waiting for the transfers outside the Strait, limiting the availability of very large crude carriers (VLCCs) for the other global key oil trade routes, such as the U.S. Gulf Coast to Asia.
The inefficient shuttle shipping is tying up a growing number of smaller vessels, Suezmaxes and Aframaxes, too, on the Hormuz trade.
This leaves fewer available empty tankers globally willing to travel to the Middle East to pick up cargoes in the Gulf of Oman.
The total capacity of the empty tankers going to the Middle East has slumped by some 40% since the end of August, per data from Tankertrackers.com cited by Bloomberg .
There are “not enough vacant tankers to take oil out of the region,” Tankertrackers.com’s co-founder, Samir Madani, told the publication.
“It’s one thing to bring the oil out into the Gulf of Oman via the Strait of Hormuz, but it seems like there isn’t enough to take the oil out of the Gulf of Oman,” the analyst said.
As of November 16, the combined capacity of ballasting supertankers and Suezmaxes en route to the Gulf of Oman has slumped to 71 million barrels, down from 130 million barrels capacity at the end of August, according to data compiled by Tankertrackers.com.
To be sure, flows from the Middle East remain elevated, albeit somewhat lower so far in November compared to October. Crude oil exports from the Strait of Hormuz have held so far despite the worst month for attacks on tankers in the area since the war began.
The high crude oil export levels despite increased security risks give the market and many analysts confidence that the only path forward is continuous recovery and, ultimately, an oil glut within months.
Tanker rates have dropped from the record highs seen in early October, but they remain above historical norms and pre-war levels amid heightened war insurance premiums and security risks.
“Security risks continue to weigh on tanker operations in the Gulf,” Maria Bertzeletou, Senior Market Analyst at Signal Group, wrote in an analysis this week.
“Repeated attacks continue to restrict the pool of owners willing to accept Gulf employment, while elevated war-risk insurance costs and operational delays add to voyage expenses and limit effective vessel availability.”
So far this month, Iran has been reporting nearly daily incidents of tankers hitting naval mines in corridors that Iran has designated as “unauthorized” in the Strait of Hormuz.
Non-Iranian observers and organizations also report more frequent attacks on tankers in and near the Strait of Hormuz.
Five tankers have been struck near Hormuz in the week between November 11 and 18, according to remote-sensing intelligence by Windward .
“This highlights Iran’s continued strategy of maritime attrition, and it is unlikely to ease unless diplomatic conditions change,” the maritime intelligence firm said on Wednesday.
Despite the threat to tanker shipping in the Strait of Hormuz, investment banks and the International Energy Agency (IEA) expect the crude oil market to be in a surplus as early as this quarter.
“We continue to expect the oil balance to loosen as supply recovers, limiting the scope for a sustained rebound in prices,” ING’s commodities strategists Ewa Manthey and Warren Patterson said in a Wednesday note.
In its November monthly report , the IEA said that the global oil market will return to a surplus this quarter, with a more substantial build in 2027.
“As always, downside risks to the forecast persist, as attacks on shipping undermine maritime security, which is pivotal to a sustained recovery,” the agency noted.
Goldman Sachs Research’s latest forecast calls for oil prices easing gradually in 2027 as suppliers in the Middle East adapt to disruption from the war in Iran.
Goldman’s commodities analysts expect Brent Crude to average $88 per barrel in 2027 under their base case assumption of no definitive diplomatic breakthrough in Iran and no re-escalation with major long-term damage to oil infrastructure.
Under the same base case scenario, Goldman Sachs forecasts that Brent will fall from around $92 per barrel today to $78 by early December 2027 “as a sizable surplus decreases Brent’s fair value from $90 per barrel today to the high $70s by the end of 2027.”

An Iranian resident looks out the window of his damaged home after Israeli-American strikes destroyed residential buildings in Tehran in April. Photograph: AFP/Getty Images
An Iranian resident looks out the window of his damaged home after Israeli-American strikes destroyed residential buildings in Tehran in April. Photograph: AFP/Getty Images
Senate Republicans rejects war powers bill to halt fighting in Iran
Measure fails 48-51 with GOP members again defending war that played a role in costing them midterm elections
The Senate on Thursday rejected a war powers resolution aimed at forcing Donald Trump to halt fighting with Iran, with Republicans once again defending a conflict that played a major role in their sweeping midterm election losses.
The House of Representatives had approved the resolution in September, and it was the first to be voted on by either chamber since the 3 November vote in which the GOP lost control of both chambers of Congress beginning next year.
The measure failed in a 48-51 vote that broke largely along party lines, with John Fetterman of Pennsylvania the sole Democrat to oppose it, and Susan Collins of Maine, Rand Paul of Kentucky and Lisa Murkowski of Alaska the only Republicans to vote in favor.
Democrats have introduced a steady stream of war powers resolutions since the war began in February with a joint US-Israel attack on Iran. While Trump’s Republican allies have succeeded in voting many of them down, one passed both chambers in June .
However Trump ignored that resolution, prompting Democrats to continue their efforts to make use of the 1973 law to force an end to a conflict that polls indicate is unpopular with the public and has caused prices for gasoline and diesel to increase across the US.
All House Democrats along with seven Republicans – several of whom lost re-election in the midterms – had supported the measure that came up for consideration before the Senate on Thursday. But Republicans largely stood behind the conflict, including Thom Tillis, a North Carolina senator, who is retiring at the end of the year after supporting previous resolutions, and Bill Cassidy, an outgoing senator of Louisiana, whose support was crucial for the June measure’s passage.
Chris Murphy, a Democratic senator, missed the vote, after recently suffering a stroke.

At China summit, Trump calls Putin 'my friend' amid Ukraine war
The West has been trying to isolate the Russian leader for years.
LONDON -- The image of Russian President Vladimir Putin sitting with President Donald Trump and China's President Xi Jinping was something the Kremlin leader has sought for years: to be treated as one of the top three global powers.
And in Shenzhen, he got it, at a gathering that all three leaders were eager to present as "historic." As several foreign policy experts have pointed out, it appears to have happened without Putin having to make any concessions.
The meeting lasted only around 90 minutes and produced a four-point joint declaration on "peace," even as Putin wages his full-scale war in Ukraine more intensively, a war that has already claimed hundreds of thousands of lives as it approaches its fifth anniversary.
Russian President Vladimir Putin, Chinese President Xi Jinping and U.S. President Donald Trump arrive for a trilateral meeting, November 19, 2026 in Shenzhen, China.
President Trump embraced Putin at the summit as "my friend," despite years of the West trying to isolate the Russian leader.
While Putin told Trump and Xi they all have "responsibility for maintaining international peace" and strengthening international law, his military is conducting a bombing campaign against civilian infrastructure in Ukraine, aimed at leaving millions without power and water. Drones targeted central Kyiv on Thursday even as the three leaders met.
Trump also went further. Before the cameras, he attacked the International Criminal Court (ICC), which in 2023 indicted Putin for war crimes, as being "out of control." The final joint declaration from the meeting included a point that criticized the ICC, suggesting it had abused its power.
The United States once endorsed the arrest warrant for Putin. The ICC did not have an immediate response to Trump's comments.
Trump-Putin-Xi meeting updates: Leaders at historic summit chart 'different course'
As Jonathan Eyal, associate director at the London-based Royal United Service Institute, wrote : "Just about the only substantial outcome of the Shenzhen summit was the rejection of international law and institutions."
While Trump's attacks on the ICC may have been intended to defend Israel's Benjamin Netanyahu, whom the ICC also indicted for war crimes, they may have been more consequential for Putin.
Ukraine's President Volodymyr Zelensky and Special Envoy Steve Witkoff arrive for a summit of the "Coalition of the Willing", a group of Ukraine's most significant allies and supporters in Berlin, November 19, 2026.
"It's all about appearances," Boris Bondarev, a former Russian diplomat who resigned in 2022 in protest over Putin's invasion of Ukraine, told ABC News before the meeting, saying Putin has long wanted an event that confirms he is "a full member of the club" of "great powers."
Basking in front of the media afterward, taking extended questions, Putin made clear his demands for ending the war are unchanged, insisting Ukraine must surrender its eastern regions.
Crimean bridge attacked for 3rd time in a week, officials say
According to a White House official, during a telephone call into a meeting of Ukraine's "Coalition of the Willing" European allies -- at which Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy was present, along with U.S. envoy Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner -- Trump said he was "super upbeat about the prospects for peace" following the summit.

For his part, Zelenskyy emphasized U.S. and European cooperation in comments following the Coalition meeting as crucial to ending Russia's war with Ukraine.
"Together, we must take the necessary steps to ensure that Russia engages in serious, substantive work instead of wasting time," Zelenskyy said, in part. "And we do not want Russia to drag all of this out into the winter. Pressure is needed. Europe is ready with new sanctions and new steps to support Ukraine and the Ukrainian people. It is important that the United States of America exert its influence on Russia."
Kremlin media has framed the Shenzhen meeting as a Yalta 2.0, a reference to the 1945 Yalta Conference between Josef Stalin, Franklin Roosevelt and Winston Churchill after World War II that divided postwar Europe, placing many countries under Soviet occupation.
Russian President Vladimir Putin speaks during a press conference following a trilateral meeting with the Chinese and US presidents on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation Economic Leaders' Meeting in Shenzhen, China, November 19, 2026
While the images of a congenial Putin and Trump will likely have caused worry in Europe and disgust in Ukraine, ultimately the meeting's immediate impact is unclear.
Ukraine and Europe have been developing ways to mitigate Trump's scaling back of support. That was illustrated by Ukraine's strikes this week, using Ukrainian- and European-made missiles, that partially collapsed Putin's bridge to Crimea .
But the meeting in Shenzhen may also have reinforced Putin's perception that the war is going his way.

items.title: After Putin talks, Trump tells Europe it could save lives and cash if Ukraine war ends - POLITICO.eu
items.summary: After Putin talks, Trump tells Europe it could save lives and cash if Ukraine war ends  POLITICO.eu
items.content:
BERLIN — U.S. President Donald Trump told Ukraine’s European allies on Thursday they could save money as well as lives by ending the war with Russia, according to five European officials who were briefed on the discussion.
In a call from Air Force One on his way home from meeting with Russian President Vladimir Putin, Trump lamented what he characterized as the waste of billions to provide Ukraine with weapons and cash for a conflict that is killing so many people, according to three of the European officials, who were granted anonymity to describe a private meeting.
Hours after concluding his encounters with the Russian leader and Chinese President Xi Jinping in Shenzhen, China, Trump had one message for the leaders gathered in Berlin: Putin is serious about negotiating a peace deal with Ukraine.
Momentum for a peace deal has grown in recent weeks after a flurry of diplomatic activity and intensive talks in Europe, Russia and the Middle East. Trump’s meeting in China with Xi and Putin alarmed some of Ukraine’s allies and raised fears that the U.S. president could be won over to the Russian argument that Ukraine and its European supporters have prolonged the war, which began with Russia’s 2022 invasion.
Some of the officials familiar with the call described Trump’s tone as strongly critical of Europe’s ongoing support for Kyiv, while others said he was just communicating in his usual forthright style. One person briefed on the call said the president had merely emphasized how much all countries could save if the war ended and Europe no longer had to pay for aid to Ukraine.
A U.S. official briefed on the call said any suggestion that Trump had told leaders to stop funding Ukraine was “not accurate.” The president was making his long-held view clear that he “wants to bring this conflict to a close,” the official said.
A White House official rejected characterizations of the call as critical of Europeans, saying: "President Trump called into the Coalition of the Willing meeting today and was super upbeat about the prospects for peace and praised the leaders in the room. The President emphasized that the war is extremely costly in terms of human life and financing, and everyone should all be striving for peace because it will save lives and money that can be invested in our countries’ own defenses and prosperity."
Trump’s argument was that if the war ends, European governments could be spending their money on rebuilding Ukraine or on their own people, the U.S. official said. The president sounded “optimistic” about the prospects for peace and praised the European leaders on the call for their efforts, the official added.
When asked at a press conference following the coalition meeting in Berlin whether Trump held too rosy a view of Putin’s desire to end the war, U.K. Prime Minister Andy Burnham said it was “quite the opposite” and that Trump had talked about the “horrific” loss of life in the nearly five-year war.
Trump envoy Steve Witkoff, who attended along with Trump’s son-in-law Jared Kushner, said the U.S. president had "adamantly supported” a peaceful end to this war and this had been his message to Putin and Xi.
“He sent Jared and I here specifically to be a part of the Coalition of the Willing, and he’s given us instructions on doing everything possible to end this war and be supportive of that effort,” Witkoff told reporters in Berlin. “And what I heard from him on the call today, was that he mentioned these very same principles to the other two leaders he was meeting with.”
Kushner emphasized that Trump wanted to make a deal with Europe fully involved in the process and had asked the two U.S. envoys to travel to Berlin to “reassure people” about that. The next talks will involve Europe joining Ukraine, Russia and the U.S. at the negotiating table, Kushner said.
He added that Putin is now ready to accept the notion of security guarantees for Ukraine similar to NATO’s Article 5 — a mutual defense pledge by allies to help defend each other if one of them is attacked.
Speaking to reporters later, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said he was “not sure” all sides had the same understanding of Article 5 as he did. “Because what does it mean, Article 5? That there are some forces of partners on your land. So, my question is: What about American soldiers?” He said Ukraine “would be happy” if the U.S. would put bases in Ukraine “like in the Middle East.”
Germany Chancellor Friedrich Merz said at the press conference, however, that Europe is providing funding for Ukrainian defense “to enable peace negotiations in the first place and to conduct them from a position of strength.”
Merz added: “We are not providing this strong support to prolong the war. We want to end this war.”
Poland’s Prime Minister Donald Tusk said Trump’s faith in Putin’s goodwill was “unshakeable” but added that he hoped this time it proved to be well-founded.
“We had a call with President Trump, who was just leaving China,” Tusk said in Berlin after the coalition meeting. “He shared his impressions of his meetings with Presidents Xi and Putin and made some remarks that sounded fairly optimistic, although I have to say they were received in the room with very cautious optimism when it comes to Putin’s and Moscow’s intentions regarding peace talks.”
“But I have to say, I’ve heard this very often from President Trump. I mean, his belief in Putin’s goodwill seems unshakable, even though so far there are no facts to support it. But it would be nice, it would be good, if it really turned out, sooner or later, that Russia was genuinely ready to engage in peace talks.”
This article has been updated with additional details. Alex Gangitano contributed to this report from Washington, James Angelos contributed from Berlin and Bartosz Brzeziński contributed from Brussels.

items.title: China issues Mount Fuji warning as family of missing climber offers reward
items.summary: The $75,000 reward offered by Chen Jie's family has sparked fears of more reckless climbing attempts.
items.content:
Image caption, The $75,000 reward offered by Chen Jie's family has sparked fears of more reckless climbing attempts
The Chinese embassy in Japan has warned its citizens against off-season ascents of Mount Fuji amid concerns that the hefty reward offered by a missing hiker's family could encourage more reckless climbing.
Chen Jie, 25, vanished on 8 November on the mountain. His family is offering 500,000 yuan ($75,000; Â£57,300) to anyone who finds him alive, and 100,000 yuan to anyone who recovers his body, say Chinese and Japanese media reports.
Strong winds and blizzards pose serious risks during the closed season, especially as shelter and first-aid centres are not operational, the embassy said on Tuesday.
Mount Fuji's official climbing season runs from around early July to early September.
Earlier this year, authorities of Yamanashi province, where the northern part of Mount Fuji sits, had said that people who attempt to climb Mount Fuji during off-peak seasons and then require rescue by helicopter will have to pay for the service from next year on.
Authorities will also require those looking to scale Fuji during the off-season to submit detailed climbing plans.
"We hope that these measures will cause people to rethink what climbing Mount Fuji during the winter is like," Kotaro Nagasaki, the prefecture governor, said at the time.
On Wednesday, Nagasaki told reporters that attempts to find the missing climber could lead to "secondary disasters"
According to Japanese news outlet the Mainichi Shimbun, Nagasaki appeared to appeal to Chen's family, saying: "I understand that your family is important, but please refrain from doing anything that could endanger others."
Some social media users in Japan have similarly expressed fears would entice people to venture into the mountains ill-prepared and lead to more accidents,
Yamanashi police said Chen had set out on his hike on 8 November with two friends, who turned back after they realised the mountain was closed and that they weren't suitably equipped for the conditions of the trails.
Chen pressed on alone from the fifth station of the Yoshida Trail, which sits at around 2,300m (7545ft) above sea level.
A friend last heard from Chen at 10:30 that day, when he sent a video message saying: "I'm going up the mountain... There's no one in sight."
The highest point of Mount Fuji, which is Japan's tallest peak, stands at 3,776m.
Local authorities launched a search for Chen on 10 November, but it had to be halted several times because of poor weather.
Chen's father reportedly arrived in Japan on 13 November. It is not clear when he posted the reward offer.

items.title: US army warns detonation of unstable explosives will create toxic plume
items.summary: The Army has delayed the controlled explosion of unstable lead azide in eastern Iowa to Monday after concerns from residents and lawmakers.
items.content:
Image caption, The US Army says that detonating the unstable materials in place is the safest option to dispose of the degrading substance
The US Army is set to detonate five tonnes of degraded explosive material in Middletown, Iowa, and have urged locals to vacate the area or stay indoors for their safety.
The detonations will result in an air plume that could send toxic dust, containing lead particles, over eastern Iowa and into neighbouring Illinois, with the potential for contaminants to settle on farmland, playgrounds and other surfaces, the army said.
The two controlled explosions will be powerful enough that they could damage buildings and shatter windows nearby.
On Thursday, environmental groups sued in an effort to stop the detonations, arguing the army failed to consider safer alternatives or give adequate notice.
The detonation was originally scheduled for noon local time (1800 BST) on Friday at the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant (IAAAP) in Middletown - a community of about 360 people about four hours west of Chicago, Illinois.
The plant produces medium- and large-calibre munitions for the US Department of Defense.
On Thursday evening, Acting Secretary of the Army Adam Telle delayed the detonation to Monday, saying that "public safety is the Army's top priority".
The planned detonation will be "the latest possible moment prior to a forecasted temperature drop, which would risk further destabilization of the material", he said on X.
The army said that the detonation is part of "a planned and controlled safety operation" to dispose of degraded lead azide. It added that the detonation has been permitted by the US Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) under conservation and recovery laws.
Residents have been asked to leave their homes for about six hours - between 08:00 and 14:00 local time - while the operation takes place and the dust settles. The army said that "all humans" should avoid outdoor activities within affected areas.
Residents in Middletown will hear a loud noise, feel vibrations from two consecutive, rapid detonations and will see a plume of dust, the advisory said.
According to Iowa Public Radio , external , the IAAAP found earlier this year that the lead azide - a highly volatile compound used as a detonator - stored in underground concrete tanks is degrading, becoming too unstable to safely move.
Military and environmental officials determined that detonating it in place is the safest way to eliminate the explosive safety hazard.
The EPA, which granted an emergency permit to detonate 68 drums of the material, said it did so because the explosion risk "presented an imminent and substantial threat to human health and the environment".
Justine Barati, a public affairs specialist at Army Sustainment Command, said that the substance has been stored at the plant for more than 20 years in earthen-covered containers.
It sits in a bath of ethanol and water to keep the material stable, but a routine check earlier this year found that some of the water had evaporated, Barati told the Associated Press.
The army said the lead azide barrels will be detonated inside earth-covered magazines made of concrete, and surrounded with barriers full of sand. The soil above will be saturated with water in an effort to reduce the lead in the air.
On Thursday, two environmental groups sued to block the detonation, challenging the validity of the EPA's emergency permit, according to the BBC's US media partner CBS News.
"The EPA itself admits that there is no safe level of lead exposure for humans," said Michael Schmidt, General Counsel at the Iowa Environmental Council.
"When our federal government makes decisions that result in a potentially toxic plume of lead dust that could cover much of southeastern Iowa, Iowans deserve to know that every available alternative was considered before choosing this method of disposal."

Taiwan's stock market fell 6.2% on Friday to cap its worst week since 1991. South Korea's KOSPI closed down 5.2% and Japan's Nikkei 225 dropped 5.1%. All three lost more than 5% as the selloff in AI chip stocks that began on Wall Street ran through a full Asian session. On Thursday the Nasdaq Composite fell 2.3% and the S&P 500 2.0% after Advanced Micro Devices sank 7.7% on a short seller's report.
For the week, Taiwan's Taiex lost 17.5%, the KOSPI 7.9% and the Nikkei 7.7%. Bloomberg called it Taiwan's worst week since 1991. Reuters reported during the session that MSCI's index of Asia-Pacific shares outside Japan was down 8.3% for the week, its worst since March 2020.
The closes read as a sign that sellers stayed in control to the end: Seoul and Tokyo finished lower than they stood at midday, and the Nikkei closed at its low of the day. That reading has a limit. Tokyo is shut Monday for a holiday, which gave traders a reason to sell before the weekend, and U.S. futures point to a smaller loss on Wall Street than Thursday's.
The Taiex closed at 36,033.29, down 2,394 points. It has lost 7,642 points since last Friday.
The KOSPI closed at 4,869.96, down 268 points, its lowest close since Jan. 16. It was down 4.6% at midday . The exchange paused program selling for five minutes on the KOSPI before noon and on the Kosdaq in the afternoon.
The Nikkei 225 closed at 56,436.65, down 3,008 points. That is a seven-month low and 23% below its 52-week high. The index was down 4.5% at the lunch break . The broader Topix lost 3.9%.

items.content:
Vladimir Putin, Xi Jinping and Donald Trump pose for a photo at the first ever meeting of the leaders of the US, Russia and China. Photograph: Win McNamee/Getty Images AsiaPac/AP
Vladimir Putin, Xi Jinping and Donald Trump pose for a photo at the first ever meeting of the leaders of the US, Russia and China. Photograph: Win McNamee/Getty Images AsiaPac/AP
New page in history? Xi, Trump and Putin summit was more of a footnote
Far from the grand ambitions declared in Yalta in 1945, Shenzhen felt like a meeting in search of an agenda
It is arguably true, given it was the first such meeting of the leaders of China, Russia and the US, that Thursday’s gathering in Shenzhen deserved the description of “historic”.
But in terms of tangible outcomes, it is unlikely to warrant the “new page in the history of diplomacy” that Vladimir Putin claimed had been written, and will instead be consigned to a smallish footnote in any future volume of the 21st century.
It’s true that the meeting could yet be an icebreaker and the start of a permanent new dialogue. It’s also true that each leader can return home with something from the 90 minutes they spent together.
Troublesome trio: Trump, Xi and Putin hold historic meeting - The Latest
Despite falling asleep during the main Apec summit, Donald Trump had a chance to show his proximity to two authoritarian leaders he admires. With Ukraine having destroyed Russia’s bridge into Crimea , the US president greeted Putin as not just a friend but almost a wartime ally.
The Russian president, although occasionally pushed to one side by protocol during the early photo opportunities, will be able to show back home that it is Moscow, and not his adversary Europe, let alone Ukraine, that commands the respect and attention of Trump and Xi Jinping . As such, the summit was a free gift to Putin, and underlined that Trump was no longer the leader of the free world, as the former British foreign secretary Jeremy Hunt commented.
From Putin’s perspective, a meeting in Berlin of the coalition of the willing was a sideshow. Europe’s attempts to isolate Russia had failed and the Asia-Pacific region had become the centre of the global economy, Putin boasted. His relationship with Trump, he said, despite the difficulties, was founded on “similar civilisational values”.
‘It’s my friend!’: Trump hails ‘great relationship’ with Putin at Apec summit – video
For Xi, it was a prestigious chance to play host and implicitly demonstrate that the era of American hegemony is over. No longer the sole arbiter in world affairs, the US, the consumer economy, must share the stage with China , the manufacturing giant, and Russia, the energy bank.
The trio’s brief joint statement covered four pretty disparate topics: boosting energy supply, reforming the United Nations, limiting the powers of the international criminal court (ICC) and a tentative commitment to discuss nuclear disarmament and non-proliferation.
Xi Jinping. Photograph: Sergey Bobylev/Sputnik/Kremlin pool/EPA For grandeur at a time of various global crises, these ambitions hardly matched Yalta in 1945 or even the declaration after the Tehran summit in 1943, when the leaders of the UK, US and Russia sat on the veranda of the British embassy and pledged that their countries would work together after the war to build a “world family of democratic nations” free of tyranny and oppression. Winston Churchill declaimed in Tehran: “In our hands we have the future of mankind.” Joseph Stalin went further. “History has spoiled us,” he said. “She has given us very great power and very great opportunities.”
Shenzhen, by contrast, felt like a meeting in search of an agenda. The vacuum was filled with platitudinous commitments to “maintain strategic stability and international security”, a task that – looking around the world – none of those in attendance are currently pursuing with great effect.
Winston Churchill, Franklin Roosevelt and Joseph Stalin at the 1945 Yalta conference. Photograph: Universal Images Group/Getty Images Perhaps technology, multipolarity and their own divisions mean even they do not have “very great power”. Certainly there were no accompanying plans for how to reform the UN, let alone boost energy production or show respect for international law – a subject Trump’s current favoured successor, Marco Rubio, had just disparaged in a speech as a plaything of the global elite.
Global courts under attack and four more takeaways from the Trump, Xi, Putin meeting
It was the summit’s chief instigator, Putin, who was the most eager of the three to set the meeting in a historic context, describing China, Russia and the US as the victors of the second world war, in a deliberate slight to Britain. A pledge to “preserve and strengthen the system of international law” seemingly referred to ensuring certain world leaders were freed from the prospect of the ICC serving them with arrest warrants.
By coincidence, the other world court, the international court of justice (ICJ), found a state – Myanmar – guilty of genocide for the first time on the same day. The Shenzen statement did not name the ICJ as a target, beyond an oblique reference to the ICC and “other similar institutions”. Doubtless that is only because ICJ rulings can be dismissed with near impunity.
Xi, nervous that China’s status as protector of the global south might be damaged by being involved in a global superpower carve-up, stuck to a familiar script: “History tells us that when major powers are at peace, the world is secure. When they clash, there is chaos.”
It may be that behind the scenes, or at other events, serious progress is being made on how China might act as a guarantor of a peace deal with Iran, or on who should lead the UN through its coming phase of reform, or even on how Putin might bring himself to seek peace in Ukraine in a way that protects Ukrainian sovereignty.
For the moment, though, it looks as if what little history was made in Shenzhen was made for exclusively the wrong reasons.

items.title: Anthropic becomes one of world's most valuable public companies in stock market debut
items.summary: Anthropic is the first purely AI company to be publicly listed, creating a test for the entire industry.
items.content:
Figure caption, Watch: How did Anthropic's stock market debut unfold?
By Kali Hays ,Â  Technology reporter Â  and Â  Rachel Clun ,Â  Business reporter
Anthropic has become one of the most valuable public companies in the world after its shares began trading on the stock market, taking its valuation to roughly $1.76 trillion (Â£1.34 trillion).
The artificial intelligence (AI) company's Thursday debut on the Nasdaq stock exchange was a crucial test for the industry, given the huge amount of money being poured into advancing the technology.
Anthropic's shares flew past its allocation price of $83 each , showing there was plenty of excitement around AI.
Yet the company, which is behind AI chatbot Claude, will remain under intense scrutiny in the months ahead to answer the key question surrounding AI: is it all worth it?
In just a few hours of trading, Anthropic's stock seemed to show that investors remain uncertain of where exactly AI is heading. The share price rose immediately to $111.53, sending the company's market value to almost $2 trillion, before falling by the end of the day as the shares closed at $97.17.
Some investors said Anthropic's debut seemed to be a success, as shares rose roughly 17% during the day, but the broader tech market did not perform as well.
The tech-heavy Nasdaq Composite Index closed down nearly 2.3%. Stocks fell in the largest tech firms, including Google's parent company Alphabet, which was down by 2.9%, while Amazon lost almost 3.9%.
The buildout happening around this era of AI is among the most expensive endeavours in the history of technology, with more than $1 trillion being spent in the last year alone by a handful of major tech companies.
The speed at which investment has grown has led to ongoing concerns of a financial bubble.
"Bubbles don't burst on the day of the largest deal," Richard Whittle, an economist with the University of Salford said. "They burst later, if the positive future becomes suspect."
Image caption, Anthropic has made one of the fastest trips from start up to IPO in history
While the basics of the technology have been around for decades, the more recent advent of more powerful computers and related components have allowed the processing of more data than ever.
The result has been AI chatbots that simulate human speech and operate tasks like software coding, digital image generation, and searching the internet more quickly.
It represents a new way of using computers that has led to the rapid rise of Anthropic, which started just five years ago and is best known as the maker of the popular AI chatbot Claude.
As the first purely AI company to go public, Anthropic will almost certainly see significant swings in price on the stock market going forward, according to Ben Barringer, who leads technology research at Quilter Cheviot.
The "initial exuberance" will wear off, Barringer said, pointing to what happened with SpaceX earlier this year.
That company, led by Elon Musk, saw shares jump by about 10% on the first day of trading, taking the company to a record-breaking valuation of $2.2 trillion.
Within a month shares had fallen below their debut price, and have mostly fallen further since.
Most tech companies see their shares fall after hitting the stock market, often after reporting quarterly results for the first time.
But many such companies, including Meta, Amazon and Google, have gone on to become the largest and most profitable corporations in the world.
With Anthropic, investors are not only looking at a notable tech company with a major valuation, and a potentially big future in business, but a company that is the first of its kind on the stock market.
"There's no obvious peer to compare it to," Neil Wilson, an investor strategist at Saxo UK, said.
Simon Jack: Can Anthropic's record-breaking IPO stop the AI bubble bursting?
So, as individual investors and even researchers and investors at large funds ask themselves if Anthropic is really worth more than $1.7 trillion, or even more, there will be few answers available.
"We'll have a stab at it," Wilson said. "I don't think anyone really knows."
A few things will likely impact the company's success on the stock market in the near-term.
One of those things is the prospect of new laws governing the use of AI tools. In the US, where Anthropic is based, Democrats will be in many more positions of power come 2027, and several politicians have already said they will be looking to ensure AI tools are safe and have some guardrails attached.
Such regulation is currently unlikely at the federal level. US President Donald Trump on Thursday spoke about AI during the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit in China, alongside Chinese and Russian counterparts, Xi Jinping and Vladimir Putin.
Trump reiterated his position against "any form of robust regulation" around the technology, adding, "we won't allow that to happen, frankly."
The same day, however, a bipartisan group of US lawmakers formed the House AI Safety and Innovation Caucus, which will work specifically on AI regulation and safety considerations.
A significant driver of this kind of scrutiny is Anthropic itself. Company executives, including co-founder and CEO Dario Amodei, have been outspoken in their purported fears that future AI tools will become so capable they will outsmart humans, to the point where extinction is possible.
Anthropic has always put itself forward in public as an AI company that takes the safety of its technology very seriously.
Daniela Amodei, Anthropic's president and sister of Dario Amodei, boasted on Thursday that the company "had an AI safety team before we launched our first product".
Despite the company's claims that the technology it is building at a rapid pace could be dangerous, Anthropic has made one of the quickest trips from start-up to IPO in history.

items.title: Putin scores ‘massive win’ at first trilateral meeting, rebuilding standing as Ukraine war grinds on
items.summary: Putin was positioned as an equal beside the leaders of the U.S. and China, handing a win to the authoritarian leader bogged down in a multi-year war.
items.content:
Putin rebuilds standing in Xi’s orbit as Ukraine war grinds on
Putin was positioned as an equal beside the leaders of the U.S. and China at a historic trilateral summit, handing a win to the authoritarian leader bogged down in a multi-year war.
It remains unclear what, if anything, was settled in the high-stakes meeting between the three leaders, with neither Kyiv nor European officials in the room.
The trilateral meeting amounted largely to diplomatic theater that elevated Russia above its true weight, with Putin signaling interest in continuing the format.
In this pool photograph distributed by the Russian state agency Sputnik, Russia's President Vladimir Putin, China's President Xi Jinping and US President Donald Trump pose for photos as they arrive for a trilateral meeting at Kylin Villa on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) Summit in Shenzhen, in China's southern Guangdong province, on November 19, 2026.
Russian President Vladimir Putin came away from China stronger than he arrived, standing as an equal beside the leaders of the U.S. and China, both far more powerful than Russia, even as he remains bogged down in a war in Ukraine now in its fifth year.
Putin stood shoulder to shoulder with U.S. President Donald Trump and Chinese leader Xi Jinping on a red-carpeted stage Thursday after the first-ever meeting between the three leaders. Trump publicly praised Putin as "my friend" as the two entered a separate bilateral meeting.
Putin was greeted at the APEC summit with smiles and handshakes, and he held bilateral meetings with at least seven world leaders over the two days. This came with the Ukraine war showing no signs of ending, more than four years after Russia invaded its neighbor.
"It's a massive win for Putin," said Joerg Wuttke, an expert at DGA-Albright Stonebridge Group. It's "as if the world has forgiven."
Hours before the three-way meeting, Ukrainian forces struck the bridge linking Russia to Crimea, a peninsula annexed by Russia in 2014, for the third time this week. Russia retaliated with a major attack on Kyiv, killing several people and damaging Ukrainian infrastructure.
The two-day summit appeared to be a symbolic triumph, even as Moscow escalated the war and took a hard line during the European Union leaders' renewed push to end the conflict.
Despite few concrete outcomes, the first-ever three-way summit is "arguably a diplomatic victory for Moscow," said Andrius Tursa, an advisor for Central and Eastern Europe and Russia at Teneo. Putin will likely seek to institutionalize the format, Tursa said.
During the meeting and afterward, Putin and Trump railed against the International Criminal Court, which has had an arrest warrant out for Putin since March 2023. Trump called the court, which his administration has sanctioned, an out-of-control "rogue globalist organization." Putin said he would consider attending the December G20 meeting in Miami after discussing it with Trump.
The three leaders issued a joint declaration of peace after the trilateral talks. Beijing has repeatedly called for negotiations and a political settlement while avoiding condemnation of Russia's aggression.
Russia the 'biggest winner' in trilateral talks: Control Risks
Putin later spent much of a press briefing after the trilateral meeting defending Moscow's decision to invade Ukraine, insisting that its root causes lie in NATO expansion and the alleged illegitimacy of Ukraine's leadership.
He also blamed the continued conflict on Ukraine's reluctance to accept terms. "If they truly want to end the conflict, they should agree to the compromises ... We accepted those terms; now, it is up to Ukraine."
This stance leaves "little scope for a ceasefire, let alone a durable settlement, absent a material shift in the military balance or political leadership in Moscow or Kyiv," Tursa said.
Russia lags both the U.S. and China in economic clout, population size, and most other major metrics of influence. Russian media, however, portrayed Putin's participation in discussions on global issues alongside the leaders of two major economic and military powers as a recognition of Russia's global power status and a setback for Western isolation efforts.
Putin said that all three leaders agreed that it's a "useful format," and such meetings could take place again.
"A key Kremlin objective will be to institutionalize such a great-power format," said Tursa. No concrete agreements on Ukraine were announced following the summit, and it remains unclear what, if anything, was settled with neither Kyiv nor European officials in the room.
One signal is whether the three leaders meet again in the near future, with the upcoming G20 summit in Miami a potential next opportunity, Tursa said.
Ukraine and European governments have said repeatedly that they must have a say in any talks on their security. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said ahead of the summit that big powers tend to assume they can decide the world's future, which he called a "huge mistake."

Stock Market Today, Nov. 19: Dow Plunges 1,100 Points as the S&P 500 Suffers Its 6th Straight Day of Losses
Wall Street's sell-off intensified on Thursday, November 19, as selling pressure spread across nearly every sector of the market. The Dow Jones Industrial Average (DJINDICES:^DJI) plunged more than 1,100 points, falling 2.19% to 49,097 and moving closer to correction territory. Meanwhile, the S&P 500 (SNPINDEX:^GSPC) fell 2.00% to 7,177, marking its sixth consecutive session of losses, while the Nasdaq Composite (NASDAQINDEX:^IXIC) dropped 2.23% to 23,886 as investors continued to retreat from growth stocks.
Selling pressure extended beyond equities, with gold falling 2.10% to $3,663.50. The 10-year Treasury yield eased three basis points to 5.07%, offering little relief to equity markets. Energy and consumer staples were among the few sectors to finish in positive territory, gaining 0.14% and 0.04%, respectively, while industrials plunged 2.61%.
Despite the broader market sell-off, Insmed (NASDAQ:INSM) surged 20.58% following reports that French pharmaceutical giant Sanofi (NASDAQ:SNY) is considering an acquisition of the biotechnology company. Palo Alto Networks (NASDAQ:PANW) also bucked the broader trend, gaining 6.42% after reporting stronger-than-expected quarterly earnings and announcing a $4.5 billion acquisition.
Conversely, Advanced Micro Devices (NASDAQ:AMD) plunged 7.72% following a media report alleging ties to a blacklisted Chinese server manufacturer. The report adds another layer of regulatory uncertainty to a semiconductor industry already grappling with tightening U.S. export restrictions and deteriorating investor sentiment.
Perhaps the most concerning development on Wall Street is how broadly selling pressure has spread. What initially appeared to be a pullback driven by elevated technology valuations is increasingly developing into a broader market downturn. Even Nvidia 's (NASDAQ:NVDA) exceptional quarterly earnings have failed to reverse sentiment, suggesting that concerns surrounding inflation, interest rates, and stock valuations are taking precedence over strong corporate results.
Looking ahead, investors should pay particularly close attention to Treasury yields and the U.S. dollar. With the Federal Reserve signaling that further interest rate hikes may be necessary, persistently restrictive financial conditions could put additional pressure on corporate earnings and stock valuations heading into 2027.
Walmart's (NASDAQ:WMT) upcoming quarterly earnings report will also provide an important assessment of consumer spending heading into the holiday shopping season. While recent results from Target (NYSE:TGT) and TJX Companies, Inc. (NYSE:TJX) have been encouraging, any signs of weakening consumer demand could introduce another headwind for equities.
For a meaningful recovery to materialize, investors should look for improving market breadth, stabilizing Treasury yields, and the S&P 500 reclaiming its 200-day moving average. Until then, investors should be cautious about interpreting isolated rallies as signs of a broader market recovery.

Trump China trip: Iran and Ukraine not in 'peace declaration' and more takeaways
Trump, Xi and Putin don't have much to say after their historic meeting.
President Donald Trump is headed back to Washington after a   historic trilateral meeting   with presidents Xi Jinping of China and Vladimir Putin of Russia -- the first-ever sitdown between the three global superpowers -- with no tangible diplomatic breakthroughs in hand.
Following their meeting, the three leaders released what was described as a symbolic four-point "peace declaration," focusing on reform at the United Nations, oil supply, nuclear risk reduction and opposition to what it called the International Criminal Court's "jurisdiction abuse."
The symbolic peace declaration made no mention of Russia's war with Ukraine, which is in its fifth year,   or the   war   with Iran. Both Russia and China have faced accusations by U.S. and European officials of providing satellite imagery and broader intelligence support to Iran, accusations both countries have denied.
Russian President Vladimir Putin, Chinese President Xi Jinping and U.S. President Donald Trump arrive for a trilateral meeting, November 19, 2026 in Shenzhen, China.
Trump left Shenzhen without taking questions from reporters after the meeting but announced in a post on his social media platform while traveling back to Washington that he would hold a news conference at the White House on Friday.
The three leaders affirmed their commitment that nuclear war should never be fought but announced no commitments to reduce their respective nuclear arsenals.
Trump had insisted nuclear arms control be a central topic of the summit.
President Donald Trump meets with Russian President Vladimir Putin and Chinese President Xi Jinping in Shenzhen, China, Nov. 19, 2026.
"As the world's three largest nuclear powers by far, the United States, Russia, and China are uniquely positioned to discuss how to reduce the number of nuclear weapons on Earth, and also to lessen the risk that those weapons will ever be used," Trump said in brief remarks ahead of the meeting. "The power is unbelievable, unthinkable."
"It's not an ​easy thing to do -- give them up," Trump said.
Trump also used the issue of nuclear proliferation to defend the U.S. war with Iran, repeating his assertion that Iran cannot obtain a nuclear weapon.
Xi tells Trump US must do 'the right thing' over Taiwan to avoid 'great turbulence'
"It's also vital that we cooperate to combat the threat of nuclear proliferation in other countries around the world. That's what we're doing in Iran. We're not going to let Iran have a nuclear weapon," he said.
In a joint statement released following the meeting, the three leaders said they had an "in-depth exchange of views on the current international situation" and "committed to maintaining strategic stability and international security."
Trump, Xi, and Putin said the three countries will conduct a dialogue on reducing nuclear risks and preventing the proliferation of nuclear weapons.
Russian President Vladimir Putin attends a trilateral meeting with President Donald Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping at Kylin Villa, November 19, 2026 in Shenzhen, China.
The "peace declaration" released after the meeting made no mention of Russia's war in Ukraine or the U.S.-led war in Iran.
Army postpones plan to detonate nearly 10,000 pounds of lead azide until Monday
Nidal Hasan is set to be executed. The military's other death row cases are in limbo
Xi tells Trump US must do 'the right thing' over Taiwan to avoid 'great turbulence'
"We are going to be discussing the war between Russia and Ukraine, and we already have. President Putin and I have had a long discussion today for quite a while. That's what pretty much what the discussion was about, and I think things are happening," Trump said.
For his part, Putin briefly commented on his escalating war in Ukraine during opening remarks.
"Our countries have numerous shared interests in the settlement of regional conflicts, including obviously the conflict in Ukraine. We discussed this yesterday with the Chairman of the People's Republic of China and today at the initiative of the U.S. president, we devoted significant attention to this during our bilateral meeting," the Russian president said, speaking through a translator.
President Donald Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping arrive for the plenary meeting at the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) Summit in Shenzhen, China, November 19, 2026.
The leaders also declared they plan to increase the production and supply of refined petroleum products "for the benefit of all nations" while also reaffirming the importance of the stable flow of energy.
The oil market has been roiled in the nine months of the U.S.'s war with Iran, with the critical waterway through which a fifth of the world's oil supplies has transited under constant threat. Ukrainian attacks on Russian energy facilities have further exacerbated global energy flows.
There were no signs upon conclusion of their meeting that Trump secured any agreements from Xi or Putin to help solve the Iran conflict.
President Donald Trump, China's President Xi Jinping and Russia's President Vladimir Putin participate in a trilateral meeting during the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) Economic Leaders' Meeting in Shenzhen, China, November 19, 2026.
Trump also highlighted that the three would discuss the International Criminal Court, the international body that works to uphold international law and prosecute war crimes. The Trump administration has targeted the ICC and its judges with sanctions and has sharply criticized the body.
"In another area of potential cooperation between us, I'll be suggesting ways to protect our nation's sovereignty from rogue globalist organizations such as the International Criminal Court, which has gotten out of control, which I believe we all agree has really strayed far from beyond its jurisdiction," Trump said in his opening remarks.
As part of the peace declaration, the three heads of state "recognized that the principle of state consent and respect for immunities of State officials are of paramount importance, and concurred that the International Criminal Court and other similar bodies must not abuse their jurisdiction."

California’s coastal communities on alert as biggest waves in years hit state
Hazard warnings issued throughout week after powerful swells and waves of more than 9 metres recorded
Multiple coastal hazard warnings were issued this week across California as successive areas of low pressure generated powerful swells and large breaking waves for coastal communities. Beaches and piers were closed last weekend as large waves crashed into California’s coastline. Offshore National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration buoys recorded wave heights of greater than 30ft (9 metres) last Friday. The Monterey, California, buoy recorded a wave height of 34.1ft which would make it the highest reading in 30 years.
Coastal warnings extended from last weekend through this week, with alerts extending until Friday night. Waves of 10-18ft are expected, with local sets of 18-22ft for San Luis Obispo county beaches and Santa Barbara county central coast beaches. These Pacific storm systems are also bringing unsettled conditions across the western US, with heavy rain, mountain snow, and strong winds through the coming days. Already, record-breaking rainfall affected San Fransisco on Wednesday, with heavy rain also causing 32,000 customers to lose power in Sacramento. Into this weekend, a further area of low pressure will bring considerable amounts of moisture for southern Oregon and northern California. By Sunday night, more than 100mm (4in) of rain is expected in places, with further snowfall for areas such as Donner Pass across the northern Sierra Nevada mountains.
A large wave pours over the seawall in Pacifica. Photograph: Fred Greaves/Reuters Nearly 72,000 people have been evacuated from areas of Odisha in eastern India as Tropical Cyclone Akvan approaches land. Akvan is expected to make landfall on Friday between Narsapur and Puri, prompting cyclone warnings from the India Meteorological Department for north Andhra Pradesh, Yanam and south Odisha coasts. Peak wind gusts are expected to reach 70mph, with rainfall totals through Friday and Saturday potentially exceeding 200mm for northern coastal Andhra Pradesh and Odisha.
Fishers carry a boat to a safer place along the shore before the expected landfall of Tropical Cyclone Akvan near Gopalpur in Odisha, India. Photograph: Reuters Following a Yellow Level 2 severe thunderstorm warning by the South African Weather Service on Tuesday, torrential rainfall and large hail were reported across parts of Johannesburg. The storms triggered flash flooding and caused infrastructure damage in the township of Soweto. One person died, while another remains missing after the severe storms.
