items.title: Myanmar committed genocide against Rohingya minority, top UN court rules
items.summary: The unprecedented International Court of Justice verdict concerns a 2017 military crackdown that killed thousands.
items.content:
Figure caption, Rohingya genocide: What was said in court and what happens now?
By Aleks Phillips ,Â  Anna Holligan ,Â  Reporting from at The Hague, Â  and Â  Jonathan Head ,Â  South East Asia correspondent
Myanmar has been found guilty of committing genocide against its Rohingya minority by the International Court of Justice (ICJ).
The verdict marks the first time a state has ever been found to have committed genocide by an international court.
Yuji Iwasawa, president of the UN's top court, said Myanmar had the "intention to destroy" a substantial part of the Rohingya population and engaged in "extensive destruction of evidence" to hide its crimes.
A military crackdown in 2017 killed thousands of Rohingya and forced more than 700,000 to flee Buddhist-majority Myanmar, formerly known as Burma. Myanmar denied the claims against it, saying its forces had responded to attacks by armed groups.
Bowen: Myanmar genocide verdict is historic and could have far-reaching implications
Image caption, Rohingyas at the Cox's Bazar camp in Bangladesh, where around a million refugees now reside, watched the verdict live
The court found on Thursday that "genocidal intent is the only reasonable inference that can be drawn from the evidence" it had seen.
The verdict was reached by a majority of nine votes to six among a panel of judges from around the world. The ICJ also found in favour by majority that Myanmar had violated several other parts of the 1948 Genocide Convention.
The case brought by The Gambia centred around so-called "clearance operations" initiated in 2017 in Rakhine State, where many of the Rohingya Muslim minority resided.
After fighters from the Arakan Rohingya Salvation Army (Arsa) launched deadly attacks on more than 30 police posts there, Myanmar troops, backed by local Buddhist mobs, launched a wave of violence, prompting a mass exodus of Rohingya.
Refugees recounted entire villages being burned down and the mass killing of civilians, while numerous survivors and eyewitnesses provided testimony that the Myanmar military had also raped and abused Rohingya women and girls.
The ICJ determined that around 10,000 Rohingya were "violently killed" during the clearance operation, while more than 700,000 are thought to have fled to Bangladesh by foot or by sea. The court found that approximately 815,000 had been targeted in some way.
Figure caption, Watch: Genocide judgement will 'mean a great deal' for Rohingya community
Iwasawa said Myanmar's military engaged in "indiscriminate" killings, the execution of men, "widespread" sexual violence, "extreme violence" against children and the deliberate burning of Rohingya homes.
He said the military had also attacked Rohingya as they were fleeing to Bangladesh.
Myanmar, he added, had engaged in "extensive destruction of evidence" by burning or disposing of bodies, burned and bulldozed sites that were cleared and failed to prosecute those who had perpetrated the acts of violence.
While the ICJ recognised the role Arsa played, it found there was "overlap" between an "anti-Rohingya hate speech campaign" - which portrayed the Rohingya as "sub-human" and "a violent threat" - and the clearance operations that made violence against the population more likely.
Myanmar consistently denied genocide against the Rohingya, saying its operations had targeted militant or insurgent threats in response to the Arsa attacks.
In January, government representative Ko Ko Hlaing told the ICJ that the country "was not obliged to remain idle and allow terrorists to have free reign". He said he had "no comment" following Thursday's verdict.
The ICJ also looked at the wider treatment of Rohingya leading up to the clearance operation and found that policies like limiting married couples to two children were discriminatory and aimed to erode their rights.
It said Myanmar had an obligation to pay proportionate reparations, but said an exact figure could be determined at a later date.
The court's decision was welcomed by Rohingya communities and human rights groups.
"This is like formal recognition of our suffering," says Mohammed Nowkim, a Rohingya who was driven out of Rakhine in 2017 and now lives in Canada. "The Rohingya have been waiting for justice for decades."
Human Rights Watch said the ruling was "long-awaited recognition of the suffering the Rohingya have endured".
Meanwhile, UN human rights chief Volker TÃ¼rk said the "suffering, misery and humiliation" inflicted on the Rohingya people was a "stain on the conscience of humanity". He added that the court's decision "must now translate into real action".
To implicate the Myanmar government in genocide, the court had to determine not just that terrible acts had been committed, but that there was an intent on the part of officials or arms of the state to partially or completely destroy the group.
Thursday's ruling is without precedent. Myanmar now carries the stain of being the first state to have been found to have violated the 1948 Genocide Convention.
The ICJ has only twice before ruled on claims of state-backed genocide in the years since the Genocide Convention was signed in the aftermath of the Holocaust, in both cases finding there was insufficient evidence to attribute the actions to the state.
Dozens of individuals have been found guilty of genocide, but finding their actions were at the direct behest of the state requires a higher evidential bar to prove genocide, the gravest of crimes under international law.
Image caption, Rohingya refugees were seen reacting as the ICJ verdict was broadcast on a big screen in Cox's Bazar, Bangladesh
Philippe Sands KC, a top human rights lawyer who helped bring the case, described it as an "historic judgment".
He told BBC Radio 4's World at One programme that it was "right up there with the great moments of international justice: Nuremberg, Pinochet, and others", referring to the trials of Nazi leaders following World War Two and that of the Chilean dictator, respectively.
However, the ICJ is not a criminal court and its powers of enforcement are limited. It cannot send military officials to prison, while it relies on the UN Security Council and political pressure to impose its rulings.
The ruling will, though, have implications for other genocide cases pending with the ICJ, including one brought by South Africa against Israel over its war in Gaza.
Sands said that pending case had been the "elephant in the room" during the Myanmar hearings.
He added that, while ruling against Myanmar did not mean the court would find similarly with Gaza, if it had not found Myanmar responsible, the case against Israel "would, in effect, be over". Israel says the case against it is "wholly unfounded".
Image caption, ICJ president Yuji Iwasawa said Myanmar had the "intention to destroy" a substantial part of the Rohingya population
Antonia Mulvey, executive director of Legal Action Worldwide, told the BBC that the court had not accepted Myanmar's counter-terrorism defence and had found for the first time that rape and sexual violence was an act of genocide, positions it would bear in mind for future cases.
A spokesperson for the US State Department said "the proper interpretation" of the Genocide Convention is of "paramount importance", and so is "preventing politicisation" of the International Criminal Court. "We are studying the decision to fully assess its implications," they said.
They said they share the "grave concerns over the continued abuses of human rights against Rohingya Muslims and members of other minority groups", and added the US is the "leading donor for the Rohingya refugee humanitarian response".
Following Thursday's ruling, UK Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband said the government was ordering Myanmar's defence attachÃ© be expelled and that he was summoning its charge d'affaires.
He pledged to set out "further action in the coming days to ensure those responsible are held to account" after a cross-party group of MPs called for the government to resume sanctions against Myanmar's military.

items.title: More climate money for Africa? Europe says use what's already pledged
items.summary: African countries at the UN climate summit in Turkey are demanding more funding from developed nations to help them cope with climate change.
items.content:
Image caption, Africa is pushing for adaptation finance to be tripled by 2035, from an annual $40bn (Â£30bn)
By Navin Singh Khadka Environmental correspondent, BBC World Service
In Uganda's northern Karamoja region, Elijah Lobur and his family now eat just one meal a day.
A severe drought that began in April has destroyed crops, while food brought in from elsewhere has become increasingly unaffordable.
"Seven months without rain has brought us to this point where we now live in hunger," the 44-year-old farmer, who lives with his grandmother, wife and five children, told the BBC.
"Even some of the wild plants that we used to eat have withered and dried up."
Local officials say more than 90% of crops have failed in the region, where agriculture is largely rain-fed.
Further south, in Malawi, Mathews Nkhambala has experienced the devastating effects of flooding.
In April 2024, barely a year after Tropical Cyclone Freddy devastated the country's southern region, floods displaced people in Chikwawa district.
Nkhambala fled to higher ground with his wife and four children as floodwaters swept through his village.
"As we reached a safe height, we saw our house swept away right in front of our eyes. Everything I had was gone," he told the BBC.
He lost a harvest of 15 bags of sorghum and part of his farmland. His children were so traumatised that they stopped going to school.
"They refused to go to school for many months. They were so disturbed," he recalled.
After relocating and trying to rebuild his life, Nkhambala is now facing another climate challenge - this time a lack of rain.
"This time we fear there may be no harvest. I have no clue what I will do."
A government assessment after Cyclone Freddy found that Malawi had experienced more than 50 disasters linked to storms, floods, landslides and droughts since 1980, affecting millions of people.
While Uganda and Malawi are suffering the effects of climate change and their governments are asking for assistance adapting to the new global weather patterns, they are among 23 African countries yet to submit National Adaptation Plans (NAPs) to the UN climate convention secretariat.
These are the plans that detail how climate change has affected them and the risks they face, and so help make a case for what assistance they need. Without them, experts say, it becomes difficult to secure funding.
"Our region has experienced cyclical droughts for decades, but there has been no action plan to tackle these climate impacts," said Milton Lorpia, who works for Warrior Squad Foundation in Karamoja region of Uganda.
"If only such a plan were in place and implemented, it would certainly have helped us."
Image caption, Mathews Nkhambala and his wife fear their harvest may fail this year
The African Group of Negotiators at the ongoing UN climate summit (COP31) in Turkey is pushing for adaptation finance to be tripled by 2035, from an annual $40bn (Â£30bn) baseline that it says developed countries committed to providing by 2025. The interpretation of that commitment remains contested.
The proposal was not accepted for formal negotiations at the summit, although African negotiators have continued to push for it.
The funding is intended to help vulnerable countries prepare for and withstand climate change-induced extreme weather, such as droughts, floods and wildfires.
But the European Union, one of the largest providers of climate finance, says the priority should be ensuring existing commitments reach vulnerable countries rather than setting new funding targets.
"We haven't come to the table with additional monies or additional capital. It's about what we have committed already and ensuring it's deployed," Darragh O'Brien, who leads the EU delegation at COP31 on behalf of the Irish presidency of the Council of the EU, told a press conference.
He acknowledged that developing countries faced difficulties accessing available funding, saying the process needed to be improved.
Wopke Hoekstra, the European Commission's climate commissioner, also argued that the summit should focus on delivering existing pledges rather than making new ones.
"If you are a vulnerable nation in the Pacific or one of the LDCs (Least Developed Countries) and the money is in the bank but does not land on the ground then it is effectively meaningless," he said.
'It can kill us': Kenyans fear impact of El NiÃ±o with floods predicted
Hoekstra said the EU had provided $30bn of the $100bn in climate finance committed by developed countries in recent years, adding that other wealthy nations should contribute more.
The scale of the need is substantial. According to the UN's Adaptation Gap Report published last year, sub-Saharan Africa requires about $51bn annually in adaptation finance, while the Middle East and North Africa needs $112bn.
Globally, developing countries will need about $300bn annually by 2035, according to the UN's latest report. Yet they received only about 10% of that amount from developed countries in 2024.
Climate-related loss and damage in Africa is projected to cost $440bn between 2020 and 2030, according to Nairobi-based think tank Power Shift Africa.
Under the 2015 Paris climate agreement, developed countries are required to provide financial support to developing nations, including for climate adaptation.
But why have so many African countries failed to prepare plans that could help them identify their needs and build resilience?
"If you look closely, the countries that are yet to submit their NAPs are already dealing with multiple crises, including debt distress, economic pressures and other issues," said David Abudho, climate justice lead at the aid agency, Oxfam.
"Their governments' ability to invest in climate adaptation is limited."
Sheila Apiny, regional climate justice adviser at ActionAid, said the lack of plans reflected a wider shortage of financial and technical support.
"The absence of NAPs in so many countries is, in itself, evidence of an adaptation finance and capacity gap," she argued.
She said this created a vicious cycle - countries lack support to prepare their plans, while not having the plans makes it harder to secure funding for climate resilience.
"When countries lack adequate adaptation planning and, more importantly, the resources to implement those plans, governments are forced into a cycle of responding to disasters instead of preventing or reducing their impacts," said Amos Wemanya, senior climate adviser at Power Shift Africa.
"Instead of investing in early warning systems, climate-resilient agriculture, water security and flood protection, scarce public resources are repeatedly diverted towards emergency relief and reconstruction. This costs more over time and leaves communities increasingly vulnerable."
Image caption, Under the 2015 Paris climate agreement, developed countries are required to provide financial support to developing nations, including for climate adaptation
African negotiators acknowledge that adaptation plans help countries prioritise investments and attract funding, but argue that their absence should not be used to deny them financial support.
"Of course, having a comprehensive NAP helps countries prioritise investments and prepare proposals for climate finance," said Mahlet Eyassu Melkie, a senior strategic adviser to Ethiopia's COP32 presidency.
"But Africa's adaptation financing needs are based on scientific assessments, climate vulnerability, national priorities and regional estimates â not simply on whether every country has submitted a particular planning document."
The UN Development Programme, which has helped more than 45 countries prepare their plans, said NAPs can help governments mobilise international support and coordinate climate action.
Fred Njehu, a Pan-African political strategist at Greenpeace Africa, said their absence could nevertheless create significant obstacles.
"It is fair to acknowledge that missing adaptation plans act as a major functional barrier that severely bottlenecks the speed, volume and quality of international funding a country can access," he said.
But having a plan does not guarantee the money needed to implement it.
"Even countries that have completed their NAPs have not received money anywhere near what they require for implementation of their adaptation plans," Apiny said.
Kenya offers an example of how adaptation measures can help communities cope with climate pressures.
Image caption, The walls of the sand dams store water underground when the rivers dry up
In the country's arid and semi-arid south-east, concrete sand dams slow the flow of seasonal rivers, allowing sand to accumulate and store water underground. Communities can access it during dry periods using hand pumps or by scooping it out.
UK charity Sand Dams Worldwide and its local partner, the Africa Sand Dam Foundation, said they had built about 1,300 such dams, improving access to water as droughts become more frequent and intense.
But many vulnerable communities elsewhere on the continent are still waiting for similar interventions.
Back in drought-hit Karamoja, Lobur wonders how different things might have been if farmers had access to small-scale irrigation schemes.
"We do have some underground water sources in some places. If there were proper plans and programmes, we could have tapped them to grow food, but we are having to live in hunger instead," Lobur said.
"My grandmother keeps reminding us how she lost eight children during a famine-like situation in 1982, and we all fear we might perish like that too."

US Oil and Gas Deal Boom Lures BMO Back Into the Market
Bank of Montreal (BMO) is jumping back into U.S. oil and gas investment banking six years after abandoning the business, apparently finding the American energy sector considerably more attractive now that companies are spending billions buying up each other.
BMO Capital Markets is hiring Ali Akbar from Mizuho Financial Group to lead its rebuilt U.S. energy practice, Reuters reported Thursday, citing people familiar with the plans. Other Mizuho bankers are expected to join him next year.
Akbar specializes in pipelines and other midstream infrastructure.
BMO exited U.S. oil and gas investment banking in late 2020, when pandemic lockdowns had devastated petroleum demand, crude prices briefly turned negative, and dozens of American energy companies filed for bankruptcy.
American energy companies are spending billions on acquisitions. Just this week, Diamondback Energy agreed to pay approximately $5 billion in cash and stock for Double Eagle's remaining interest in a Midland Basin partnership. Deals like this generate business for investment banks by advising buyers and sellers, arranging financing, and underwriting securities.
BMO's return is about investment banking only and should not be mistaken for a reversal of some wholesale abandonment of fossil fuels. In fact, BMO's overall fossil fuel financing increased 25% between 2020 and 2021, reaching $23.5 billion, according to figures published by Investors for Paris Compliance.
The bank also revised its coal policy in November 2023, removing a statement that restricted coal financing amid scrutiny from West Virginia over financial institutions accused of boycotting energy companies.
BMO's latest move doesn't necessarily mean the bank will increase direct lending to oil producers, but it is a clear sign that BMO sees enough prospective business in American oil, gas, and pipeline transactions to justify rebuilding an entire team it dismantled six years ago.

items.content:
Andy Burnham at a roundtable with business leaders in Brussels on Friday. Photograph: Hannah McKay/Reuters
Andy Burnham at a roundtable with business leaders in Brussels on Friday. Photograph: Hannah McKay/Reuters
UK and EU close to post-Brexit deal as they agree 100,000 youth mobility cap
Two sides find provisional compromise on scheme but food and farming negotiations go down to the wire
British and European negotiators were closing in on a reset deal on Thursday night as they provisionally agreed to allow 100,000 EU citizens to come to the UK every year under a new mobility scheme.
It is understood the EU dropped its demands at the last minute that its students should pay home tuition fees if they attended British universities in a concession to get the deal over the line.
The UK had strongly resisted EU text on the table committing it to home fees instead of “significantly reduced” international fees, but a compromise was hammered out before 10pm, with a “supplementary agreement” to work out the details within the next six months.
Brussels insiders said the EU had kicked the can down the road and agreed not to mention the tuition fees rate in the declaration, with further negotiations to follow in the next six months.
As talks went into the night, EU sources suggested both sides were on track for an agreement within the next day.
Burnham and European Commission president Ursula von der Leyen at a summit in Dublin this month. Photograph: Stefan Rousseau/Reuters On Friday morning, the UK prime minister, Andy Burnham , said the UK and Europe were “stronger together”, adding: “The test for this summit is simple: does it make life better for people in Britain? That is what I will deliver in Brussels today – cutting costs, keeping prices down in the supermarkets and creating opportunities for young people.”
The Reform UK leader, Nigel Farage, told the BBC that Burnham’s approach amounted to a “betrayal”. He said: “He’s trying to do it incrementally but it’s perfectly clear that this very very soon becomes a debate about do we rejoin or do we stay out.”
But he acknowledged that for food exporters a deal on agricultural standards would make things “a little bit easier”.
On the eve of a summit in Brussels, the EU was “going into a landing zone” on the question of a British voice in shaping the rules under a food and drink agreement the government hopes to unveil on Friday, an EU source said.
There also seemed to be a compromise by France after a dispute among member states over how far Britain could be involved in shaping policies related to the food and drink deal.
The UK had demanded a “voting” role on some law-making in relation to food standards that France heavily opposed, and London eventually conceded on a point many think was unrealistic from the start. Instead, the UK will be consulted on new food laws, but the details on the level of involvement remain to be seen.
Earlier on Thursday the UK made concessions to increase the quota of EU citizens who could take part in a new youth mobility scheme, agreeing a cap of 100,000, instead of 50,000-80,0000 as previously sought.
It was also agreed to raise the age cap from 30 to 31.The number of young British people allowed to go to the EU under the scheme will be matched but could be higher, with some countries, including Germany, being prepared to take unlimited numbers each year .
With less than 24 hours to go before Burnham was due in Brussels for the summit with EU leaders, the two sides still needed to resolve some sticking points.
Speaking in general terms about the disagreements, another EU diplomat said: “It will go down to the wire. Our feeling is that the Brits have to move if they want a deal.”
A spokesperson for the British prime minister also described the talks as close, saying if an agreement was reached, the government would bring forward legislation, the cutting costs bill, to parliament next week.
The Guardian view on Europe and Burnham: a future that can only be viewed through a glass darkly | Editorial
At the long-awaited summit, the EU and UK hope to sign three agreements, which are expected to add 0.4% to British GDP , including the highly prized food and drink deal that was a Labour manifesto commitment.
The deal, expected to come into force on 1 March 2028, requires the UK to align with EU rules on sanitary and phytosanitary (SPS) standards, making Britain a rule taker.
Asked about Britain’s status as a rule taker, No 10 said the Labour manifesto had aimed to build closer ties with the EU, adding: “We were obviously elected on a manifesto that promised to reset the relationship and seek to deepen ties with our European friends.”
According to EU sources, the UK has been pushing to have a formal role in EU committees involved in implementing existing and setting new SPS rules. An EU diplomat said: “They want to be able to shape decisions, not only implementation, but future decisions. That has always been a red line.”
Under the SPS proposal, the UK will agree to dynamically align with EU laws and will have a “voice” but “not be in the room” when laws are drafted.
A second diplomat from a country sympathetic to the British position said the European Commission had proposed an “extremely restrictive consultation mechanism” for the UK.
In contrast, the EU diplomat thought it was reasonable for a British representative to take part in the implementation of SPS legislation affecting the UK. “Of course the UK cannot vote in the council as a non-member state, but we feel that we need to be pragmatic about coordination and implementation,” they said.
The issue proved difficult to resolve because it divided member states. France was perceived by other member states to be the main barrier to greater UK involvement in EU working groups on food and drink laws. “They are super principled on that point,” said a second EU diplomat.
The French government does not agree that it has been the main block, arguing that only a few member states wanted to accommodate the UK.
The issue raises the tensions at the heart of the UK’s status as a rule taker, and would be many times magnified were Britain to choose to enter the single market as a non-EU member state. The precise details of how the UK would be consulted on future food and farming rules remain unclear.
Andy Burnham is in danger of over-selling his big Brussels summit. What happens if he under-delivers? | Joël Reland
Burnham’s spokesperson suggested there was a UK-EU consensus that there would be no further incremental reset summits beyond the one on Friday until a full negotiation commenced on a longer-term, more stable relationship, such as rejoining the single market.
“After the summit, we will begin those discussions with our European partners about the realistic options for our longer-term relationship,” he said.

Senior Tories urge Badenoch to drop Brexit talk in major strategy shift, sources say
Exclusive: While PM pushes for EU reset, Tory leader is moving away from ‘divisive’ issue that defined party for years
Kemi Badenoch has been advised by her team to limit the amount of time she spends discussing Brexit and Europe, the Guardian has been told, moving the Conservatives away from an issue that defined the party for many years.
While the Tory leader still gives views on Brexit – in an opinion piece in the Daily Mail on Thursday she condemned Andy Burnham’s ongoing reset with the EU as a “backwards” move – sources say it is now seen as a second-order subject.
Instead, Badenoch intends to focus on areas the party believes are more fertile electoral ground, in particular the economy, the cost of social security and defence.
One source said Badenoch had been advised to shift the narrative away from Brexit by Stephen Gilbert, a former Conservative official who is now a peer and who joined the Tory leader’s team as a senior political adviser a year ago.
Although another party source said Gilbert’s advice was “more nuanced” than this, Badenoch’s recent run of speeches and interventions appears to demonstrate the change.
In eight sets of prime minister’s questions since Burnham entered No 10 over the summer, Badenoch and her deputy, Alex Burghart, who took one session when Burnham was away, have focused on Europe just once, on 28 October, when she challenged the PM on whether or not he wanted a new Brexit referendum.
Every other outing has focused on various aspects of the welfare state, the cost of living, or defence, also including subjects such as the budget, debt and whether or not the UK should drill for more North Sea oil and gas.
“The way I see it, this is less of a conscious attempt to sideline Europe than it is a way to talk more about the subjects we think are our strong points, like the economy and defence,” one senior Conservative said.
One Tory shadow minister said the wider party was firmly behind the idea: “Europe does still come up from time to time, but as a former remainer even I think we should move on. I’m not sure what is likely to change by us talking about it all the time.”
Another shadow minister said: “We don’t want to be talking about Brexit for multiple reasons – including the simple one that it was so awfully divisive.”
Will Burnham put ‘brake’ on push to rejoin EU? | Politics Weekly
Badenoch does still at times defend Brexit to selected audiences, for example in Thursday’s Daily Mail piece, where she disputed Burnham’s charge that it had hampered the UK’s economic growth , saying the prime minister “wants to reopen arguments from 2016 because he has no answers for the world as it is”.
At other times her language on links with the EU has been more nuanced than the period when the Conservatives liked to disparage the continent as economically moribund and less relevant than more distant economies.
Asked about Burnham’s attempt to renegotiate the post-Brexit trade agreement during a press conference on defence earlier this month, Badenoch said: “They say they want to end red tape on food checks – that’s a good thing”, while then predicting this would not actually happen.
Badenoch also said she accepted that the deal with the EU could and should be updated: “The free trade agreement that we have with the EU, like many others, is one that needs constant negotiating. So I want to see Labour negotiating and improving on deals with all countries. That’s what you do when you have your own trade policy.”
A Conservative spokesperson said: “As Kemi has said, the last thing the country needs is to be dragged back into a debate on Brexit. That absolutely does not mean Kemi and the Conservatives won’t discuss the EU, but we will be very clear that Andy Burnham is only trying to reopen old wounds on Brexit because he doesn’t have anything to say about the challenges facing the country.
“Bringing down the welfare bill, funding defence, cutting taxes to promote growth can all be done outside the EU. Burnham’s reset is one big distraction and we will never shy away from saying so.”
